card.name: Cowboy Hat
card.subject: A tan-brown cowboy hat with a wide curled brim and a tall creased crown.
card.hero_colors: tan brown, cream, small red hatband

errors.what: The two sides of the brim do not match. A cowboy hat's brim is a roughly oval sheet, curled up about equally on both sides. Here the left side is broad, rounded and almost flat. The right side curls up and narrows into a pointed horn-like tip. Viewing angle cannot explain the difference, so the brim reads as lopsided rather than as one symmetrical oval.

The hatband's ring is drawn too flat for the angle the brim is seen from. The brim is seen well from above: its front edge drops far below the band and we see a lot of its upper surface. So the round base of the crown and its band should look clearly oval, with a deeper downward curve at the front. Instead the band's lower edge bows only slightly, almost like a ring seen at eye level. As a result the crown looks a little more side-on than the brim it sits on.

card.name: Cowboy Hat
card.subject: A tan-brown cowboy hat with a wide curled brim and a tall creased crown.
card.hero_colors: tan brown, cream, small red hatband

errors.what: The two sides of the brim do not match. On a real cowboy hat they are mirror images that curl up the same way. Here the left side is a short, rounded curl, while the right side runs about twice as far from the crown and ends in a sharp, wing-like point. A felt brim cannot hold that shape, and the three-quarter view does not explain the difference. As a result the crown sits well off-centre on the brim.

The crown faces the camera almost straight on, so the two sides of the brim should look about the same. Instead the left half is a broad, flat surface seen from well above, and the right half is a thin, upturned, pointed edge seen almost edge-on. The two halves read as two different views, or two different brim shapes, rather than one symmetric brim under one camera.

The hatband's curve is fairly shallow and the crown's sides are drawn nearly level. Together they suggest a lower viewpoint than the left brim, which is drawn widely open from high above. If the brim were seen from that high, the band would curve more strongly and more of the crown top would show.

card.name: Cowboy Hat
card.subject: A tan-brown cowboy hat with a wide curled brim and a tall creased crown.
card.hero_colors: tan brown, cream, small red hatband

errors.what: The two sides of the brim should be mirror images, but they differ. On a real cowboy hat both sides curl up the same way and keep a rounded oval edge. Here the left side is wide and rounded, while the right side tapers into a sharp upswept point, like a horn or wing. Felt brims cannot form a point like that, and the three-quarter view cannot explain it: the far side of the brim would look shorter, but it would still be rounded.

The brim's upper face is seen steeply from above: its oval is open, about half as tall as it is wide. The crown is drawn close to eye level. Its top shows only a side silhouette of the front pinch, with no view down into the crease that runs front to back, and the band's ellipse is flatter than the brim's. Those two parts read as two slightly different camera heights.

The left and front brim is wide and seen face-up. The right side shrinks to a narrow, nearly edge-on wing that sweeps up to a point. On a symmetric brim seen from one three-quarter view, the left side should curl to match. As drawn, one side looks flat from above and the other looks seen from the side, so the brim's outline is not one consistent ellipse.

card.name: Cowboy Boot
card.subject: A brown leather cowboy boot with a tall shaft, pointed toe, angled heel and a small spur.
card.hero_colors: saddle brown, dark brown, small gold spur

errors.what: The spur has nothing holding it on. A real spur has a U-shaped heel band that wraps around the back of the heel on both sides, plus a strap over the instep fastened with a buckle or button. Here a single straight gold bar leaves the rowel and stops in the middle of the side of the foot, as if glued on. It is a loose end with no attachment, so the spur would fall off.

The heel is drawn in three-quarter view. Its back face shows as a wide slanted parallelogram, and its bottom edge drops below the sole line. The sole and toe beside it are pure side-on profile, so the heel is seen from a different camera angle than the rest of the foot.

The top opening is an open ellipse that shows the inside lining, as if seen from above. The sole is a flat edge-on line at eye level with no top or bottom surface showing. With a single slightly-high camera, the sole and heel should show a hint of their top planes and turn in the same direction.

card.name: Cowboy Boot
card.subject: A brown leather cowboy boot with a tall shaft, pointed toe, angled heel and a small spur.
card.hero_colors: saddle brown, dark brown, small gold spur

errors.what: The spur's heel band stops in a bare rounded tip on the leather. There is no strap button, and no spur strap runs over the instep and under the arch, so nothing holds the spur on the boot. It looks glued to the side of the heel rather than strapped on.

The heel's visible front face and the hint of lining say the camera is slightly above. At that height the opening should read as a narrow ellipse, with the far inner wall showing across the whole width. Instead the rim is drawn as a flat profile outline, and the lining shows only in a small notch at the front-right. The top is not seen from the same height as the heel.

The spur arm is a straight rod that ends in a rounded cap in front of the boot's side. It does not curve around the back of the heel the way a real spur band hugs the counter. So it does not follow the curved surface it should rest on, and it reads as floating beside the boot rather than strapped to it.

card.name: Cowboy Boot
card.subject: A brown leather cowboy boot with a tall shaft, pointed toe, angled heel and a small spur.
card.hero_colors: saddle brown, dark brown, small gold spur

errors.what: The spur's heel band stops in a blunt tip on the side of the foot. There is no spur strap over the instep, no strap button and no buckle, so nothing holds the spur on the boot. It reads as a bracket stuck onto the leather rather than a spur strapped around the heel.

The opening is not drawn as an ellipse matching the round shaft. Most of the top, from the back to the left side, is a closed, rounded, dome-like rim, and only a small notch of lining shows at the front-right. A round tube seen slightly from above, as the visible lining says it is, should show one oval opening across the full width of the shaft, with the back rim seen over the inside and the front rim in front of it.

The spur arm is a straight flat bar lying on the side of the boot and stopping in a rounded tip. It does not curve around the round heel. A yoke that wraps the heel should show as a curved band following the boot's surface and turning out of sight around the back and the far side.

The ankle seam is an almost straight slanted line, while the top rim curves as if seen from above. Under one camera placed above the boot, a ring lower down on the boot should bow downward toward the viewer at least as much as the top rim. Here the lower ring reads as seen level and the top as seen from above.

card.name: Lasso
card.subject: A coiled yellow-tan rope with a big open loop on one end.
card.hero_colors: golden tan, cream, small red tie

errors.what: The loop is drawn as a closed ring joined into the honda. In a real lasso the honda is tied at the rope's end and the standing part slides through it to form an adjustable loop. Here no rope passes through the eye: the rope from the coil and both ends of the loop all end inside the honda. The loop could not slide or tighten, so the lasso cannot work.
The tail bends sharply out of the middle of the coil's lower turns and melts into them. It does not peel off the outermost turn, so you cannot tell which strand it continues.
The coil's turns blend into one another and have no clear start or end. The rope that runs to the honda grows out of the coil's side without coming off a single traceable turn.

card.name: Lasso
card.subject: A coiled yellow-tan rope with a big open loop on one end.
card.hero_colors: golden tan, cream, small red tie

errors.what: The honda is drawn as a plain bead with rope passing through it on both sides. No rope end is tied or spliced into it. In a real lasso the end of the rope is fixed at the honda and the rope runs through it to make the noose. Here the noose looks like a closed ring threaded onto a bead, so it is unclear how the loop could be pulled tight.

The tail bends straight out of the front wrap and seems to merge into the coil, instead of clearly being the last turn coming off the coil. The coil's inner wraps also stack into a crescent rather than reading as separate round turns.

The coil's turns fan out sideways like a tilted stack, showing its side, yet its outer edge and inner hole are drawn as nearly round circles. A stack tilted enough to show its side would have narrower, oval edges. The noose loop and tail beside it lie flat and face-on, so the coil looks like it was seen from a more sideways angle than the rest of the lasso.

card.name: Lasso
card.subject: A coiled yellow-tan rope with a big open loop on one end.
card.hero_colors: golden tan, cream, small red tie

errors.what: The coil is not made of separate, even turns. The strands are thick and clearly separate on the right but thin out and merge into one crescent on the left, so the turns melt into each other instead of reading as distinct loops of one rope.

The strand that runs to the honda has no clear starting point. It seems to come out from behind or inside the coil rather than continuing from the outermost turn, so the rope's path from the coil to the noose cannot be followed.

The two parts suggest slightly different viewpoints. The open loop is a horizontal ellipse, squashed top to bottom, as if it lies on the ground and tilts back from the viewer. The coil's opening is an almost perfect circle, as if seen straight on, yet its turns slide sideways as if seen from the left. The two rings lie on the same ground, so they should be foreshortened the same way. This is mild and fits the stylized look, but it shows on a close look.

card.name: Saloon Doors
card.subject: A pair of short swinging wooden doors with slatted tops and a gap at the bottom.
card.hero_colors: warm brown, light wood, small gold hinges

errors.what: The left door is slightly skewed against the right door. Its thick right edge and down-sloping bottom rail suggest it is swung open, yet its two hinges stay flat against the post face as if it were closed. The two leaves don't quite read as mirrored doors hanging in one plane.

The bottom of the frame is seen turned at an angle, but the top is seen straight on. The right foot is about 80 px lower and noticeably bigger than the left, so the right side is nearer. Yet the lintel is perfectly level, the same thickness at both ends, and seen square-on. Both post tops sit at exactly the same height, and both posts are the same width. As a result the right post is drawn longer than the left, and the line through the feet does not run parallel to the lintel, even though those edges are parallel on the real object. The top and bottom of the doorway come from two different cameras.

The floor is seen clearly from above. The posts and lintel show almost none of their top or side faces, as if seen level and straight on. This leaves the frame looking pasted onto the turned floor instead of standing on it.

The two doors are not lined up with each other. The right door hangs clearly lower than the left: its bottom rail sits about 30 px below the left door's. The left door's top and bottom rails tilt in ways that don't match a door swinging on its hinges. The right door is completely flat and front-on, and its bottom does not follow the lower-on-the-right slope that the feet set up.

card.name: Saloon Doors
card.subject: A pair of short swinging wooden doors with slatted tops and a gap at the bottom.
card.hero_colors: warm brown, light wood, small gold hinges

errors.what: The frame's top and bottom are drawn from two different views. At the bottom it is turned with the floor: the right foot sits much lower, so the right post is nearer and longer. At the top it is flat-on to the camera: the lintel is perfectly level and both post tops are at the same height. If the frame is angled, the lintel should slant to match the floor line and the planks, and the nearer right post should rise higher at the top as well. Instead the lower half recedes and the upper half faces the viewer.

The right door is a flat front-facing rectangle: its hinge edge and free edge are the same height and its rails are level. It ignores the frame's turn shown by the floor and post feet, and it does not match the left door, which is drawn swung toward the viewer.

The left door looks rotated a little within the picture, as if tilted, rather than swung on its vertical hinges. Its free edge leans slightly off vertical, and its bottom rail slopes much more steeply than its top rail, which a hinge swing does not produce.

card.name: Saloon Doors
card.subject: A pair of short swinging wooden doors with slatted tops and a gap at the bottom.
card.hero_colors: warm brown, light wood, small gold hinges

errors.what: The pair is supposed to be mirrored, but the leaves don't match. The left leaf is about 15% shorter than the right one. Its bottom rail sits well above the right leaf's, and its hinges are at different heights from the right leaf's hinges. The left leaf is swung toward the camera, so perspective should make it look the same size or larger, not smaller. As drawn, the leaves could not close flush as a pair.

The left leaf's hinge stile overlaps the front face of the post instead of hanging inside the opening, at the post's inner face. The leaf looks pasted in front of the post rather than pivoting beside it, which a real hinge would not allow.

The right door faces the camera flat: its top rail, bottom rail and middle rail are level, and its slats are equal and straight-on. The frame it hangs in is turned, with the base line sloping down to the right, and the left door follows that slope. So the two doors read as two different views: the left one in perspective, the right one pasted on front-on. The right door's rails should slope down toward the near post like the bases and floor planks, and its slats should widen slightly toward the near side.

The top beam is perfectly level, while the post feet step down sharply to the right, which makes the right post noticeably taller than the left. The frame becomes a trapezoid whose top ignores the turn shown at the bottom. A beam this high would at least slope slightly the same way, and its top face, seen faintly from above, conflicts with treating it as sitting on the horizon.

card.name: Star Badge
card.subject: A gold five-pointed star badge with a small ball on each tip.
card.hero_colors: gold, yellow, small red gem

errors.what: The five points are not even. The bottom-left arm is short and wide, while the top and bottom-right arms are long and thin. The inner corners sit at uneven distances from the centre, and the tilt alone does not explain the difference. A stamped sheriff's star is a regular star, so the badge looks slightly warped.

The domed red stone in the centre is an invented part. Real sheriff's stars have a stamped or engraved centre (a seal, emblem or the word 'SHERIFF'), not a gemstone. Game art accepts it as a stylisation, but it is not true to the object.

card.name: Star Badge
card.subject: A gold five-pointed star badge with a small ball on each tip.
card.hero_colors: gold, yellow, small red gem

errors.what: Invented part: a glossy red jewel set in a gold bezel. Real sheriff's badges have a flat or engraved centre, such as a seal, an embossed small star or a lettered disc, not a gemstone. The jewel turns the badge into a piece of jewellery or a magic amulet.

card.name: Star Badge
card.subject: A gold five-pointed star badge with a small ball on each tip.
card.hero_colors: gold, yellow, small red gem

errors.what: The five points are not regular. The lower-left point is clearly shorter and stubbier than the others, and the gaps between points vary. The tilt is too slight to explain this, so the star looks lopsided instead of symmetric like a stamped metal badge.
The red jewel in the centre is an invented part. Real sheriff stars have an engraved or embossed centre seal or lettering, not a gemstone.

card.name: Saddle
card.subject: A brown leather horse saddle with a raised front horn, curved seat and a dangling stirrup.
card.hero_colors: chestnut brown, tan, small silver buckle

errors.what: The seat top, horn cap and stirrup treads are all seen from clearly above. The square rail they rest on shows only its front face, with almost no top face, as if seen at eye level. The rail's camera height doesn't match the saddle's.

card.name: Saddle
card.subject: A brown leather horse saddle with a raised front horn, curved seat and a dangling stirrup.
card.hero_colors: chestnut brown, tan, small silver buckle

errors.what: The far stirrup comes out from under the near skirt on a very short stub, with no stirrup leather running down the far side of the saddle. It looks as if it hangs from the underside of the near skirt, in the space between the skirts where the rail sits, not from the far side of the tree. It also sits too close beside the near stirrup for a saddle this wide on a thick rail.
The rail's top edge on the left sits level with or slightly above the underside of the seat roll. The rail seems to pass into the saddle body instead of the gullet sitting on top of it.

card.name: Saddle
card.subject: A brown leather horse saddle with a raised front horn, curved seat and a dangling stirrup.
card.hero_colors: chestnut brown, tan, small silver buckle

errors.what: The far-side stirrup has no clear leather to hang from. It seems to come out from under the near skirt, just behind the front stirrup, rather than from the far skirt behind the rail. So it reads as a second stirrup on the same side, or as a stirrup hanging from nothing, instead of one stirrup on each side of the saddle.

The saddle is seen from the side, but both stirrup arches face the camera square-on as full D shapes, as if turned 90° from the saddle. On a saddle seen side-on, the stirrup arches should be turned with the fender and seen partly edge-on, as narrow ellipses, with the treads running across the fender.

The far stirrup hangs just behind the near one, under the middle of the near fender, almost the same size and at the same angle. It does not hang from the far-side skirt behind the rail, so both stirrups read as hanging on the near side instead of one on each side of the saddle.

card.subject: A round wooden barrel with dark metal hoops and a flat lid.
card.hero_colors: wood brown, dark gray hoops, small orange stain

card.name: Barrel
card.subject: A round wooden barrel with dark metal hoops and a flat lid.
card.hero_colors: wood brown, dark gray hoops, small orange stain

errors.what: The stave seams above the hoop do not line up with the seams below it. A real stave runs unbroken from top to bottom under the hoops, but here, on the right side especially, the seam spacing changes across the hoop, as if different boards start above and below it.

The head looks like a lid laid on top of the staves, level with or slightly above their ends. On a real barrel the staves stand a little above the head, which sits in a groove inside them. This is acceptable as a simplification and only shows on a close look.

The barrel is seen from only a little above its lid: the top ellipse is narrow and the hoops curve gently. The floor is drawn as if seen from a noticeably higher camera. It is spread out, with a lot of visible depth between the barrel's base and the wall, and the plank lines are steep and widely spaced rather than squeezed flat as a low camera would show them. The object and its ground do not quite share one viewpoint.

errors.what: The head looks like a separate lid laid on top of the barrel: a disc with its own raised rim that sits on the stave ends. On a real barrel the head is set into a groove just below the top of the staves, so the stave ends rise slightly above it. As drawn, the head does not look held in place by the staves.

card.name: Covered Wagon
card.subject: A wooden wagon with a rounded white canvas cover and two large spoked wheels.
card.hero_colors: white canvas, wood brown, small red trim

errors.what: The seat plank is drawn level and runs left to right. It also reaches past the front-left corner of the box, so its left support stands in empty space in front of the cover. A seat that spans the cart's width should run along the front panel's top edge, which rises slightly to the right, and fit within the narrow front face. As drawn, it lies along the side of the cart rather than across its front.

card.name: Covered Wagon
card.subject: A wooden wagon with a rounded white canvas cover and two large spoked wheels.
card.hero_colors: white canvas, wood brown, small red trim

errors.what: The pole comes out of the outer corner of the box side. It is not centered under the front and is not fixed to an axle or undercarriage. Pulling on it would drag the cart sideways at one corner, so it could not steer or pull the cart straight.
No axle or frame is visible connecting the two wheels to each other or to the box. The hubs just sit against the side panel, so nothing shows how the box carries its load onto the wheels.

The pole ends in a T-shaped hand-pull crosspiece, but the cart also has a driver's bench, which means an animal pulls it. A horse-drawn cart would have two shafts or a tongue with a yoke. The pulling gear doesn't match what the cart is for.

The two faces disagree on which end is nearer. The long side is taller at its left end (about 145 px) than at its right end (about 100 px), and its top and bottom edges close together toward the right, so it is drawn as if the left end is nearer and the side recedes to the right. Yet the right (front) end face with the seat is also visible, and the tongue runs from that end toward the viewer. Both only make sense if the right end is nearer. The box is two views joined at the front corner.

The far wheel is shifted about 250 px to the right of the near wheel, while the front end face, which shows the cart's full width, is only about 100 px wide. Wheels on a shared axle should be offset by about the width the end face shows. This offset also points the axle along a different direction than the box edges do, so the wheels do not sit on one axle across the body.

The near wheel is drawn as an almost perfect circle with a face-on hub, while the box side it is mounted on is clearly foreshortened. The wheel should be a slightly narrower ellipse that matches how far the side face is turned.

card.name: Covered Wagon
card.subject: A wooden wagon with a rounded white canvas cover and two large spoked wheels.
card.hero_colors: white canvas, wood brown, small red trim

errors.what: The pole starts at the near bottom corner of the front panel and runs out at a diagonal, off the cart's centerline. A tongue has to sit centered under the front of the box and be fixed to the axle or undercarriage so an animal can pull straight. Pulled from one corner, the cart would yaw, and no frame member is shown under the box for the pole to attach to.

The pole ends in a short flat block lying on the dirt instead of a yoke or singletree/doubletree with hitch points. Nothing on it could connect to a draft animal, so the cart has no working way to be pulled.

The red hub is mounted straight onto the box side and no axle or axle bed shows under the body. The far wheel has no visible link to the near one either, so the wheels look stuck onto the box rather than carried on an axle.

The far wheel should sit on the same axle as the near wheel, so it should appear just behind it, shifted by the box's shallow depth (about the width of the front end face). Instead it is shifted about 250px forward toward the front end and sits much higher on the ground. That matches a cart far deeper than the box is drawn, or a second axle out of line with the first. The two wheels do not share one axle in one view.

The far wheel's bottom touches the road well above the near wheel's bottom, by much more than the slight rise of the box's front end edges. The two wheels sit on ground planes seen at different angles.

card.name: Steam Train
card.subject: A black steam locomotive with a tall funnel chimney, round front lamp and large red wheels.
card.hero_colors: black, dark gray, red wheels, small gold bell

errors.what: The headlamp is stuck to the side of the smokestack, off-centre. On a real locomotive it sits on a bracket centred on the smokebox, in front of the stack. Here it looks bolted onto the chimney.

The pilot bars do not form a consistent wedge. The leftmost bar drops straight down, and the others lean at growing angles until the right ones are almost diagonal. The bottom frame sticks out past the near rail instead of sitting centred between the rails just above them, so the pilot looks skewed rather than like a symmetric plough.

The piston rod from the cylinder ends at the first driver's face. A separate rod starts again at the middle driver, so there is no continuous main rod and crosshead linking the cylinder to one driver crankpin and the coupling rod to all three drivers. The drive linkage does not fully connect.

card.name: Steam Train
card.subject: A black steam locomotive with a tall funnel chimney, round front lamp and large red wheels.
card.hero_colors: black, dark gray, red wheels, small gold bell

errors.what: The headlamp is bolted to the side of the smokestack and juts out past the boiler front, with no bracket or smokebox mount under it. On a real locomotive the lamp sits on the smokebox top or front.

The side rod runs diagonally from low on the first driver up to the hub of the third driver. It skips the middle driver and crosses the piston rod in a V. A real side rod joins the crankpins of every driver at the same height, parallel to the rail, and the main rod runs from the crosshead to a single crankpin.

The pilot is a cage of near-vertical bars hanging straight down from the beam, with its bottom bar resting at rail and tie level. A real cowcatcher is a forward-sloping wedge that clears the rails. This one would catch on the track.

The front of the boiler is drawn as a full, face-on circle (about as wide as it is tall), yet the whole length of the boiler's side is visible going back to the right. At this three-quarter angle the round front should be an upright ellipse, clearly narrower than it is tall, like the side wheels. Instead it reads as pasted flat toward the viewer.

The running board and the bottom edge of the boiler recede at a much shallower angle than the rails below them. Extended, these lines meet well below the horizon instead of sharing the rails' vanishing point. The body seems turned away from the direction of the track, so it does not run along the rails its wheels stand on.

The cowcatcher's bars fan out at different angles, and its bottom bar does not run parallel to the buffer beam above it. The pilot does not read as one frame lying across the track in the same view as the beam.

card.name: Steam Train
card.subject: A black steam locomotive with a tall funnel chimney, round front lamp and large red wheels.
card.hero_colors: black, dark gray, red wheels, small gold bell

errors.what: The two silver rods cross each other in an X instead of forming a working linkage. One runs from the cylinder to the second driver. The other runs from near the hub of the first driver to the hub of the third. A real main rod goes from the crosshead to an off-centre crank pin, and a coupling rod links the drivers at matching crank pins. Rods fixed at or near the axle centres and crossing each other could not turn the wheels.
The cowcatcher's bottom bar reaches down to the rails and seems to sit on or below rail height. A real pilot stays a few inches above the rails; this one would drag on the track and the ties.

The body is not lined up with the rails. The deck edge and boiler axis rise at a shallow angle toward the upper right, while the rails rise much more steeply. The front of the body (buffer beam, smokebox face) is drawn almost square to the camera rather than square to the track. The wheels follow the rail line but the body above them does not, so the locomotive looks twisted on its own chassis and does not run along the track.

The smokebox face is drawn as an almost full circle and the buffer beam as a flat horizontal rectangle, as if seen straight on. But the long side of the body is shown strongly receding, which calls for a clearly narrowed ellipse and a beam that slants with the side. The front face and the side face look like they come from two different viewpoints.

The wheels are fairly open, almost front-facing ellipses that differ in roundness from wheel to wheel. On a side plane receding this steeply they should all be narrower ellipses of matching proportion, shrinking toward the back.
The slats fan out at different angles instead of running parallel and converging consistently with the front face's perspective.
